title: Fruita Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Fruita wells have a 200-foot median depth, with finished well costs commonly modeled at $16,000-$27,000.
h1: Fruita, Colorado Well Depths, Yields, and Costs
intro_html:
If you are buying land or planning a home near Fruita, the local well records give a useful starting point, but not a guarantee for one parcel. Within 5 miles of Fruita, Colorado DWR records show 354 permitted wells. Only 127 are recorded as constructed, 182 report total depth, 22 report pump yield, and 8 report a static water level.

The records point to a generally shallow water level and mostly moderate-to-good reported production. They also show a wide range of drilling conditions, including wells reaching 1,030 feet. Nearby Loma, Redlands, and Grand Junction can provide context, but your own lot, aquifer, well location, and intended use still control the final result.

sections.heading: Fruita well depths vary from shallow to very deep
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Fruita is 200 feet. The middle half runs from 15 to 300 feet, while the 90th percentile is 400 feet. The deepest record reaches 1,030 feet. Depth records are also unevenly distributed: 47% are under 100 feet, 18% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 31% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 4% exceed 600 feet.

That spread matters when comparing drilling bids. A contractor may price a straightforward shallow hole very differently from a deeper or more difficult well. The records name mostly unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, with 339 wells in that category, 8 alluvial wells, and 2 Entrada wells. In fractured ground, water-bearing cracks can be unpredictable, so nearby depth alone is not a promise for your parcel.

sections.heading: Reported Fruita well yields are generally workable
sections.html:
Only 22 wells in the records report a pump yield, so treat the production statistics as a local guide rather than a guarantee. The median reported yield is 9.5 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 5.2 and 18.8 gallons per minute. Half of the reported wells produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 32% report more than 15 gallons per minute.

Another 18% report between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, and none of the reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute. A lower-yield well can still serve a household when storage and pump sizing are handled correctly, but it gives less margin for irrigation or other uses. Confirm the permitted use, pumping test, recovery, and storage plan before relying on a yield number.

sections.heading: The Fruita water table looks shallow, but the trend is unclear
sections.html:
Only 8 wells report a static water level. Among those records, the median depth to water is 8 feet, and the middle half runs from 4 to 18 feet. That suggests groundwater may be relatively shallow at some Fruita locations, especially in alluvial settings, but it should not be read as a site-specific water level.

The permit records supplied here do not provide enough water-level observations by decade to establish a reliable rising or falling trend. Seasonal conditions, pumping, irrigation, and the exact well location can all affect a measurement. Ask for the well construction report and the measured static level for any existing well, then have a driller evaluate how that information applies to the proposed well location.

sections.heading: Fruita permit history shows long-running drilling activity
sections.html:
Permit activity near Fruita stretches from the 1950s through the newest permit year, 2024. The records list 7 permits in the 1950s, 6 in the 1960s, 2 in the 1970s, 19 in the 1980s, 74 in the 1990s, 85 in the 2000s, 56 in the 2010s, and 23 in the 2020s. That history confirms sustained development, but it does not mean every parcel has the same access to groundwater.

The most active driller names in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), Rocky Mountain Drlg./Pump Svcs (Wisener, A. L.), and Artesian Services Inc. (Himes, Brad). These are permit-record entries, not recommendations. Compare current licensing, insurance, scope of work, casing and grout specifications, testing, and references before choosing a contractor.

sections.heading: What a new Fruita well may cost
sections.html:
The local cost model assumes mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. A typical drilling rate is $50 to $75 per foot. At the 200-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $10,000 to $15,000. That is only the drilling portion, not the complete water system.

A finished well with a pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $16,000 to $27,000. The final bid can change with depth, casing and grout requirements, access, difficult ground, power distance, pump selection, and water testing. Ask each bidder to separate drilling, construction, pump equipment, trenching, electrical, testing, and any permitting or site work so proposals can be compared directly.

sections.heading: Fruita buyers should check water quality and site limits
sections.html:
The mapped area within about 10 miles contains 38 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 1 historic mine feature, and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those locations do not prove that a particular well is contaminated, but they are a reason to review environmental records and test existing or new well water. A private well owner is responsible for understanding the water quality at the tap.

Low yield, a dry hole, poor construction, and an unsuitable well location are separate risks. Confirm setback requirements from septic components, available space for a replacement or storage system, and access for a drilling rig. Domestic, stock, irrigation, and monitoring uses appear in the permit records, so confirm that the existing permit allows the use you plan. Colorado DWR requirements and any augmentation plan issues should be checked before construction or a change in use.

sections.heading: Use the records before buying a Fruita lot
sections.html:
Start with the parcel’s permit number, well construction report, pump test, static water level, water-quality results, and legal use. Then review neighboring wells, particularly on the same side of the valley or in the same geologic setting. Nearby Loma and Redlands records may help with context, while Grand Junction is farther away and may not represent the same ground conditions.

For a vacant lot, get a driller’s opinion on access, likely depth, casing and grout, pump placement, and the chance of needing storage. For an existing home, inspect the pressure system and test flow and recovery rather than relying only on a seller’s description. If the plan includes irrigation, livestock, or more than ordinary household use, verify the water right and permit before treating the well as adequate.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Fruita, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Fruita is 200 feet. The middle half runs from 15 to 300 feet, but the records range much farther: the 90th percentile is 400 feet and the deepest recorded well is 1,030 feet. Local geology and the exact parcel can produce a very different result.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Fruita?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50 to $75 per foot. At Fruita’s 200-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $10,000 to $15,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $16,000 to $27,000. Access, ground conditions, depth, and equipment can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Fruita wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 22 Fruita-area records reporting pump yield, the median is 9.5 gallons per minute and the middle half is 5.2 to 18.8 gallons per minute. Half report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, while 18% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute. The small reporting set means a test on the actual well matters.
